key_insight: Large language model–powered agents (e.g., Claude Code) can autonomously execute end-to-end high energy physics analyses — from event selection through statistical inference and paper drafting — with minimal expert-curated input. This demonstrates LLM agents can meaningfully perform substantive experimental science workflows.
problem_solved: Reduces the heavy manual effort, expertise bottleneck, and reproducibility friction in building and executing complex HEP analysis pipelines by automating routine and technical stages of the workflow.
method: Provide the agent with a HEP dataset, an execution framework (code/runtime), and a corpus of prior experimental literature.
Use the LLM-based agent to iteratively generate and run code to perform event selection, background estimation, uncertainty quantification, and statistical inference.
Have the agent synthesize results into human-readable deliverables (figures, tables, and draft paper text) with minimal human intervention.
impact: Enables faster, more reproducible experimental analyses and lowers the barrier to entry for HEP research; suggests LLM agents can augment or partially automate scientific workflows across ML-driven domains.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing sequential stages: Dataset → Agent (code execution) → Event selection → Background estimation → Uncertainties → Statistical inference → Paper draft
Interaction schematic: Agent ↔ Dataset + Execution Framework + Literature corpus (arrows showing read/write/code-run loop)
Comparison chart (e.g., bar or timeline) showing time/effort or expert-hours for traditional vs. agent-assisted analysis
Example outputs panel: sample event-selection code snippet, a summary plot, and a one-paragraph draft abstract
paper_title: AI Agents Can Already Autonomously Perform Experimental High Energy Physics
paper_authors: Eric A. Moreno, Samuel Bright-Thonney, Andrzej Novak, Dolores Garcia, Philip Harris
